chapters.title: Chapter 1: What the Forex Market Is

lessons.title: How the Rupee Gets Its Price: Interbank Market, RBI Reference Rate and the NDF Market

children.text: On 1 April 2026, the rupee was sitting near a record low of about 95.22 per dollar. The next day it closed around 93.10, reportedly its biggest single-day gain in about 12 years. India's trade deficit had not vanished overnight and FPIs had not rushed back. What changed was a set of RBI rules on how banks deal in the offshore rupee market. That episode tells you something most beginners never learn: the rupee's price is formed in more than one place, and those places constantly pull on each other. This lesson shows you all three.

body.text: The rupee does not have one price. It has a live onshore price set by banks, a daily benchmark used to settle contracts, and an offshore shadow price traded in Singapore and London. Understand how these three connect and you understand how USD/INR really moves.

children.text: Layer 1: The Onshore Interbank Market

markDefs.definition: The wholesale market where banks buy and sell currencies with each other in large sizes, usually $1 million and above. Its prices are the base for every retail rate you see.
An electronic trading screen where banks post and match currency prices. In India, the main ones are CCIL's FX-Clear and LSEG's Matching platform.

children.text: The live USD/INR rate you see on a news ticker comes from the
interbank market
. Authorised Dealer banks such as SBI, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Citi and HSBC buy and sell dollars with each other on
electronic matching platforms

and through brokers, between 9:00 am and 5:00 pm IST. Every time an importer, exporter or FPI deals with its bank, the bank adjusts its own position here. This is where the demand and supply from the previous lesson actually turns into a number.

children.text: Not every interbank deal settles at the same time. Indian dealers quote four kinds of settlement date, and the rate differs slightly for each because of the interest rate gap between India and the US.

body.title: Why does "spot" mean two days, not today?

children.text: The T+2 convention dates from a time when banks in different time zones needed a couple of days to confirm deals and move money through correspondent accounts. A dollar bought in Mumbai actually lands in a bank account in New York, and a rupee lands in India, so both payment systems must be open. Technology has shrunk the delay, but spot remains the global standard quote, which is why cash and tom rates are quoted as small adjustments to spot. You will see exactly how those adjustments are calculated in Chapter 2.
From Interbank Rate to the Rate You Actually Get

markDefs.definition: The daily list of rates a bank offers retail customers for buying and selling foreign currency, including its markup over the interbank rate.

children.text: You never get the interbank rate as an individual. Your bank buys dollars at interbank and sells them to you at its
card rate
, which includes a markup. The less efficient the channel, the bigger the markup. Buying physical dollar notes at an airport counter is usually the most expensive way to buy a dollar.

body.caption: Buying $5,000 for a trip when interbank USD/INR is 95.50 (illustrative rates)

cells: Cash notes at a forex counter

body.title: The tuition markup
body.prompt: Rahul's parents in Nagpur wire $20,000 for his first semester at a US university. Their bank charges a TT selling rate of 96.95 when the interbank rate is 95.50. How many extra rupees do they pay compared with the interbank rate?
body.explanation: The markup is 96.95 minus 95.50 = ₹1.45 per dollar. Multiply by $20,000: 1.45 × 20,000 = ₹29,000. Over a four-year degree with similar transfers every semester, the markup alone can run into several lakh rupees, which is why comparing rates is worth ten minutes of your time.

body.text: RBI built a way to narrow this gap. FX-Retail, a platform developed by CCIL and live since August 2019, lets bank customers, including individuals, buy and sell USD/INR for genuine needs such as tuition or travel at prices much closer to the interbank market. You access it through your bank, which still charges its own transaction fee, so compare the all-in cost.

body.label: CCIL FX-Retail Platform
body.description: RBI-backed platform where bank customers can deal USD/INR for genuine forex needs at near-interbank prices.

children.text: Layer 2: The Reference Rate, India's Daily Benchmark

markDefs.definition: Financial Benchmarks India Pvt Ltd, the administrator that computes and publishes key Indian financial benchmarks, including the USD/INR reference rate since July 2018.

children.text: The interbank rate changes every second. Contracts, however, need one agreed number for the day. That number is the USD/INR reference rate. Most people still call it the "RBI reference rate" because RBI published it for years, but since 10 July 2018 it has been computed and published by
FBIL

. It is built from actual interbank trades during a randomly chosen 15-minute window between 11:30 am and 12:30 pm, with outlier trades removed, and it is published at around 1:30 pm on every business day. Choosing the window at random makes it much harder for any bank to push the benchmark by trading at a known time.

body.label: USD/INR reference rate publication time
body.value: Around 1:30 pm IST, every business day
body.context: Computed by FBIL from interbank trades in a random 15-minute window between 11:30 am and 12:30 pm. FBIL also publishes reference rates for other major currencies such as EUR, GBP and JPY against the rupee.

children.text: Where this benchmark shows up:
Exchange-traded currency derivatives.
USD/INR futures on NSE and BSE settle on expiry day against the reference rate, so it directly decides your final profit or loss if you hold to expiry.
Offshore NDF contracts.
Rupee NDFs traded in Singapore and London use the reference rate as their fixing, which you will see in the next section.
Business contracts and valuations.
Companies, funds and banks use it to value foreign currency assets and settle agreements that need a neutral, published rate.

body.title: Expiry day
body.question: Sneha holds a USD/INR futures contract on NSE until expiry. At 3:00 pm on expiry day the live interbank rate is 95.62, and the reference rate published at 1:30 pm was 95.48. Which rate is her final settlement based on?
body.explanation: USD/INR futures on Indian exchanges are cash-settled against the reference rate on expiry day. The live rate a few hours later does not matter for final settlement, which is why traders holding to expiry watch the midday window closely.

children.text: Layer 3: The Offshore NDF Market

markDefs.definition: Non-deliverable forward. A forward contract on a restricted currency where no rupees change hands. At maturity, only the profit or loss is paid, in US dollars.
A currency that cannot be freely bought, sold or moved across borders for all purposes. The rupee is convertible for trade but not fully for capital account transactions.

children.text: The rupee is not a fully
convertible currency
. A hedge fund in Singapore cannot simply open an account in Mumbai and trade dollars and rupees freely. So global investors created a workaround: the
non-deliverable forward

, or NDF. Two parties agree on a USD/INR rate for a future date. On that date, no rupees move. They compare the agreed rate with the reference rate and the loser pays the difference in dollars. NDFs trade mainly in Singapore, London and Dubai, including at hours when India's onshore market is shut.

body.caption: Settlement for the buyer of a USD/INR NDF. A positive result means the buyer receives dollars; a negative result means the buyer pays.

children.text: Worked example: a Singapore fund buys a one-month $10 million USD/INR NDF at 96.00, betting the rupee will weaken. On fixing day, the reference rate is 97.00. Settlement = 10,000,000 × (97.00 minus 96.00) ÷ 97.00 = $103,093 in its favour. No rupee ever left India, yet the fund made money on the rupee's fall.

body.title: When the bet goes wrong
body.prompt: The same fund buys another $10 million one-month NDF at 96.00. This time the rupee strengthens and the fixing rate is 95.00. How many US dollars does the fund pay? Round to the nearest dollar and enter it as a positive number.
body.explanation: Settlement = 10,000,000 × (95.00 minus 96.00) ÷ 95.00 = 10,000,000 × (minus 1 ÷ 95) = minus $105,263. The negative sign means the buyer pays. Notice the loss here is slightly bigger than the gain in the worked example, because the rupee difference is divided by a smaller fixing rate.

columns.label: Onshore deliverable forward
points: Traded with Authorised Dealer banks in India
Actual dollars and rupees are exchanged at maturity
Governed by RBI rules under FEMA
Mainly used by importers, exporters and investors to hedge real exposures
Onshore hours, 9:00 am to 5:00 pm IST

columns.label: Offshore NDF
points: Traded mainly in Singapore, London and Dubai
Only the difference is paid, in US dollars
Outside India, but RBI can influence it through rules on Indian banks
Used by global funds to hedge or speculate on the rupee
Trades when India is closed, so it often signals the next day's onshore open

body.text: The onshore and offshore markets are connected through arbitrage. If the rupee is cheaper offshore than onshore, banks with access to both can buy dollars in one market and sell in the other, pocketing the gap. That trading pulls the two prices back together. When the gap blows out, it is usually a sign of stress, and RBI tends to step in.

body.title: The March to June 2026 Episode: When RBI Reached Offshore

events.title: Position cap on banks
events.description: RBI caps each Authorised Dealer bank's net open rupee position at $100 million at close of business, with compliance due by 10 April. The earlier limit was linked to bank capital.

events.title: NDF curbs
events.description: RBI bars banks from offering rupee NDF contracts to clients, restricts rebooking of cancelled rupee derivative contracts and bans such deals with related parties. Banks begin unwinding onshore-offshore arbitrage trades, reported at around $30 billion.

events.title: Rupee jumps
events.description: The rupee closes around 93.10 after touching a record low of about 95.22, reportedly its biggest single-day gain in about 12 years.

events.title: Partial rollback
events.description: With markets calmer, RBI allows banks to resume some NDF activity. The $100 million position cap stays, and derivative deals with related parties remain barred.

events.title: Fine-tuning
events.description: RBI exempts certain swap positions linked to FCNR(B) deposits and foreign currency loans from the banks' position limits, as part of measures to attract foreign currency inflows.

events.title: Pressure returns
events.description: With crude elevated and FPIs selling, the rupee trades back near 95.5, showing that rules can calm a panic but cannot override the underlying flows.

body.text: The NDF market is an institutional, offshore market. It is not a product for Indian retail traders, and RBI's rules on Indian banks' participation have changed several times, sometimes within weeks. If you are an Indian resident with a genuine currency exposure, the regulated routes are forwards with your bank or rupee-pair derivatives on NSE or BSE. Without an exposure, rupee-pair derivatives are not permitted. Chapter 4 covers the rules.

body.title: Reading the morning signal
body.scenario: USD/INR closed onshore at 95.54 on Friday. Over the weekend, a major oil-producing region sees a military escalation. At 7:30 am on Monday, a dealer at a Mumbai bank sees one-month rupee NDFs trading at a level implying spot of about 96.20. The onshore market opens at 9:00 am.
body.prompt: What does the NDF signal suggest about Monday's onshore open, why does the offshore market move first, and how might the reference rate published at 1:30 pm end up differing from the 9:00 am level?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The NDF market is pricing a weaker rupee, roughly 66 paise above Friday's onshore close, so the onshore market is likely to open with a gap towards 96 or higher.
2. The offshore market moves first because it trades in Singapore and other hubs while India is closed. Global funds react to weekend news there before Indian banks can trade onshore.
3. The 9:00 am onshore open is not the final word. Importers rushing to buy dollars could push USD/INR higher during the morning, while RBI could sell dollars through state-run banks to slow the move.
4. The reference rate is built from trades between 11:30 am and 12:30 pm, so it will reflect wherever that tug of war has settled by midday, which may be above or below the opening level.
5. Any USD/INR futures expiring that day, and offshore NDFs fixing that day, will settle against that midday reference rate, not the 9:00 am open.

body.title: How NDFs settle
body.textWithBlank: At maturity, a rupee NDF is settled by paying only the difference in US ___, with no rupees changing hands.
body.explanation: That is what makes it non-deliverable. The contract compares the agreed rate with the fixing rate and settles the gap in dollars, which lets offshore investors take rupee exposure without moving money into India.

cards.definition: The wholesale market where banks trade currencies with each other. It sets the live USD/INR rate.
Settlement today (T+0), tomorrow (T+1) and in two business days (T+2). Spot is the standard quoted rate.
A bank's retail buying and selling rate for foreign currency, including its markup over interbank.
The daily USD/INR benchmark computed by FBIL from interbank trades and published at around 1:30 pm.
Non-deliverable forward. An offshore contract on the rupee settled only as a dollar difference against the fixing rate.
A bank's overall unhedged exposure to a currency. RBI capped banks' rupee net open position at $100 million in March 2026.

points: The live USD/INR rate is set in the onshore interbank market, where Authorised Dealer banks trade with each other from 9:00 am to 5:00 pm IST.
India's onshore forex market turns over about $80 billion a day, and total rupee trading worldwide is about $185 billion a day.
Individuals pay a markup over interbank. Wire transfers are usually cheaper than cash notes, and CCIL's FX-Retail platform can narrow the gap further.
The reference rate is India's daily benchmark, computed by FBIL from a random midday window and published around 1:30 pm. Exchange-traded USD/INR futures settle against it.
Offshore NDFs let global investors bet on or hedge the rupee without moving rupees, and they often signal how the onshore market will open.
Onshore and offshore prices are linked by arbitrage, and RBI can reach into the offshore market through rules on Indian banks, as it did in March and April 2026.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment, trading or legal advice. Retail forex rates in the tables are illustrative. RBI rules on bank positions and NDF participation have changed repeatedly in 2026, so check the latest RBI directions before relying on any regulatory detail here.
